messages.text: What is this paper about and what did they find?

messages.short_answer: The paper introduces PromptScaffold, an editor that guides non-expert users to write LLM prompts through four slots (role, task, examples, output format). In a 16-participant within-subjects lab study, template prompts scored higher on automatic task scores (0.74 vs. 0.61) and raised participants' confidence, but took somewhat longer to write.

sections.title: What the editor does
sections.text: The authors describe a template with role, task, examples and output format slots, each with a short hint and example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that users can preview and edit, and a side panel shows model outputs for test inputs the user provides.

sections.title: Main findings and trade-offs
sections.text: Prompts written with PromptScaffold reached higher task scores than free-form prompts, with the largest gain on topic labelling, where most participants added labelled examples. According to the overview, participants reported higher confidence (4.1 vs. 3.4 on a 7-point scale) but spent more time (7.5 vs. 6.2 minutes). Some participants filled slots mechanically without understanding their purpose.

sections.title: Relevance to your user study
sections.text: Your focus on how non-expert users write prompts overlaps with this paper's study design, so its measures (automatic task score, confidence, time, interviews) could inform your own instruments. You might consider whether a template is a useful comparison condition, or whether you need open-ended tasks and expert ratings, since the authors list these as gaps.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: The sample was small, homogeneous and mostly computing students, the session lasted only 70 minutes, and only three predefined tasks and one LLM were used. Success was measured by automatic scores and self-report, and novelty may have inflated confidence.

sources.text: 3 The PromptScaffold Editor PromptScaffold splits a prompt into four slots. The role slot states who the model should act as. The task slot describes what to do, with a hint to name the input and the goal. The examples slot asks for one to three inputoutput pairs, and the output format slot asks how the answer should be structured. Each slot shows a short hint and an example. The editor assembles the slots into one prompt that the user can preview and edit freely before running it. A side panel shows the model's output for a small set of test inputs that the user provides. 4 Study Participants. We recruited 16 participants (9 women, 7 men, aged 19 to 27) through university mailing lists. All were undergraduate or master's students; 11 studied computing or engineering and 5 studied other subjects. None had taken a course on machine learning, and all had used a chatbot before.

Design and tasks. The study used a within-subjects design with two conditions: free-form prompting in a plain text box, and PromptScaffold. Each participant completed three predefined tasks in each condition: classifying customer reviews by sentiment, labelling support tickets by topic, and summarising short news articles in two sentences. The main outcome was an automatic task score between 0 and 1: accuracy against gold labels for the two classification tasks and a reference-based overlap score for summaries. sources.text: The paper presents PromptScaffold, a prompt editor that guides non-expert users through a four-slot template (role, task, examples, output format) with hints and a preview of model outputs on test inputs. In a within-subjects lab study with 16 university students, participants completed three predefined tasks (sentiment classification, support-ticket topic labelling, and two-sentence news summarisation) under both free-form and template conditions. The authors identify limitations including a small, homogeneous sample, a single 70-minute session, only three tasks and one LLM, and reliance on automatic scores and self-report.

messages.short_answer: Partly. Its findings are about a specific tool on predefined tasks, so it fits your project only if your research question is also about tools or measurable prompt quality.

sections.text: The authors used a within-subjects design with free-form prompting as one condition and PromptScaffold as the other, with three predefined tasks in each. They counterbalanced condition order and used parallel task versions so no participant saw the same inputs twice. They combined an automatic task score, a 7-point confidence rating, time to final prompt, and an end-of-session interview.

sections.title: Which parts may transfer to your study
sections.text: The counterbalancing, parallel task versions, and interview are reusable for a study of how non-experts write prompts. The automatic accuracy score only works for tasks with gold labels, so it would not suit open-ended prompt writing without a different quality measure.
